children: By Sarah Klearman

Hardware is back. Just ask Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado, who helps lead the firm's newly announced $1.1 billion Machine Age fund. Casado, a Stanford University Ph.D. in computer science, remembers attending Hot Chips, an annual Stanford semiconductor conference, in the early 2000s, when it was largely populated by industry retirees reminiscing about the good old days.
"If you went to Hot Chips last week, it's young and energetic," Casado said. "It's a very dynamic and evolving space. Hardware is cool again."

Casado joined Andreessen in 2016 and leads the firm's infrastructure practice, investing in computer science infrastructure like network, compute, storage and developer tools, among other things. His team led the venture firm's investments in OpenRouter, which agreed to be acquired by Stripe this month, and Cursor, purchased by SpaceX. Andreessen is expected to net north of $8 billion from its investments in the two companies, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
We caught up with Casado to understand Andreessen's philosophy for hardware investing and where infrastructure-both hardware and software-goes from here. Here are edited excerpts.

WSJ Pro: You have pointed to artificial intelligence bottlenecks and the shifting focus of founders toward hardware as the motivation for launching the Machine Age fund. Andreessen has made hardware investments before. When did it become clear there was critical mass in this category and that it deserved its own focused fund?

MC: We keep track of all the inbound leads that we have every time we have a partner meeting, which is every week. We were like, you know what? Twenty to 30% of these deals are hardware. And not only that, we're actually spending a lot of time engaging on them, because the teams are so good. The second realization was, we work with many of these [AI] companies and in every case, there's consternation around getting supply. So there's a confluence of two facts: This on the ground learning about the need, as well as the observation that founders are going toward it.

You lead Andreessen's infrastructure practice, focusing on computer science infrastructure. In prior interviews you've said infrastructure investing requires product knowledge, not necessarily technical expertise. Can the same be said of hardware?

No. I think that hardware-it's one of those things where if you build it, it'll normally work. Like, if you build a faster inference chip, you can sell it. The question is: Can you build it? And it tends to be, in my experience, a much more capital intensive and complex engineering problem to do hardware.

There is a lot of interest in hardware and physical AI. I've come across at least one venture capital investor comparing this moment for those categories to what we saw with software investment in 2021. What do you make of that?

AI requires a change in the hardware side. I'd say it's a revision back to something VC has been doing for quite a while. VC started with hardware. I don't know how to compare to 2021, because in 2021 there were a lot of external factors that didn't have to do with tech change. A lot of that was like, there's a lot of money flooding in, there was the Covid effect, a bunch of other stuff. So I think it's a bit different.
On the topic of infrastructure: Your team led Andreessen's investment in OpenRouter and Cursor. Do these transactions tell us anything about the path forward for infrastructure companies?

We're seeing the fastest-growing companies in the history of the industry with Anthropic and OpenAI. The limitation is on the supply side, not the demand side. The demand seems basically infinite. If you're in a company in the position of catering to all that demand, you're going to do anything you can to increase supply. So I think it is a setup to see more consolidation. That said, there's also plenty of room for independent companies that don't consolidate, too.

OpenRouter and Cursor both began with one business model in mind and had shifted to another, in Cursor's case a few times over, by the time they were acquired. Is that just the nature of early-stage companies, or a function of how quickly infrastructure is changing?

Well, it's both. So companies have to be very dynamic, they often pivot, that's the standard. It's just the extent they have to pivot and the time scale they have to pivot in is the most extreme any of us have ever seen. I just think this is an incredibly fast-moving industry, and the nature of it is changing very quickly. I think it's worth asking why that is, and here's my basic thesis, which is: Let's imagine a company was raising 10 years ago, and they asked for $1 billion and you gave it to them. What would they do with that money?
Hire, I guess?

They'd hire, and then they'd blow up. Because you can't scale engineering. That is actually what is changing with AI. With AI, if I give a team of 20 people a billion dollars, they could actually use it productively. The nature between capital and innovation has changed.
How would you sum up your investment thesis for infrastructure investment, whether software or hardware?

First off, we think founders are smarter than VCs, so if there's enough founders in a space, we think it's an investible space. We give less credibility to our belief whether the space will work or not and more to the founders [who] are voting with their feet. As soon as we think there's a credible argument that there's a certain team in a credible space that's the leader, we try to invest in that company. That is the approach we've taken with software, and we would use the same approach for hardware.
